title: How to Get Dog Hair Out of Car Seats and Carpets
meta_description: Why dog hair clings to car carpet, the DIY method that works (rubber glove, pet hair brush, vacuum), and when it needs a proper interior clean.
excerpt: Dog hair weaves itself into car carpet, which is why a hoover alone leaves so much behind. Here's the at-home method that works, and when it's time for a proper clean.

keywords: how to get dog hair out of car

faq.q: How do you get dog hair out of car carpet?
faq.a: Take the mats out and vacuum the loose hair first. Then loosen the rest with a slightly damp rubber glove or a pet hair brush, using short strokes in one direction so the hair rolls up into clumps, and vacuum again with a crevice tool, working against the pile. On felt-like boot carpet, a stiff pet hair brush lifts what rubber can't.

faq.q: Can a normal vacuum get dog hair out of car carpet?
faq.a: It gets the loose hair, but not the hair that's woven into the fibres. Loosen it first with a damp rubber glove or a pet hair brush, then vacuum again.

faq.q: Will a pet hair stone damage my car carpet?
faq.a: Some are abrasive enough to rough up the fibres. Test on a hidden patch, use light pressure, keep it to the boot lining and floor carpet, and don't use it on seats.

faq.q: How do I get rid of the dog smell in my car?
faq.a: Most of the smell comes from oils and dirt in the fabric, not from the hair. It needs the fabric cleaning, with shampoo and extraction, rather than an air freshener.

Hoovered the boot three times and the dog hair's still there? That's normal. Short, coarse hairs work their way into the carpet fibres, and a vacuum pulls air around them rather than lifting them out.

The fix is to loosen the hair first and vacuum it out second. Our new guide covers the at-home method that works (a damp rubber glove, a pet hair brush and a crevice tool), where DIY runs out, and how we deal with it on our jobs.
